title: Envy on the road home
hookLine: on the road home, Duryodhana confesses his envy to Shakuni, and Shakuni turns it into a plan
carry: envy is one of the six inner enemies
last: THE WOUND OPENS BEFORE THE DICE.

cards: Duryodhana is heading home to Hastinapura, and he keeps sighing. His uncle Shakuni, riding with him, notices and asks what's wrong. And Duryodhana tells him.
Not a polite version. The whole thing: the kings bowing to his cousin, the wealth flowing in, the hall that made a fool of him, the laughter. He says he can't bear it.
He says it's burning him up inside. A confession on the road, and an uncle who hears in it an opportunity.

teach.b: Listen to what Duryodhana actually says.

teach.h: SHAKUNI: A WAR THAT LOOKS LIKE A GAME.
teach.b: Not that the Pandavas cheated him. That they're prospering, and he can't stand it. Their success is the injury.
Shakuni at first does what a good friend might: don't grieve, he says; they have their fortune, you have yours. But Duryodhana won't be comforted. So Shakuni changes course.
You can't beat them in battle, he says in effect; they're too strong. But Yudhishthira loves dice, and doesn't play well. I do.
Invite him to a game, and I'll win everything he has, and you won't lift a weapon. Now the teaching. Hindu teachers have a name for what's burning in Duryodhana.
They speak of six inner enemies, the shadripu: kama, desire; krodha, anger; lobha, greed; moha, delusion; mada, pride; and matsarya, envy.
They're called enemies, not sins, because they live inside you and fight you for the wheel.
And the Mahabharata gives envy a face.

Many readers see Duryodhana as the epic's great portrait of matsarya: a prince with a kingdom of his own, made miserable by someone else's good fortune, until the feeling finds a helper and becomes a plan.
That's the teaching for today. You won't stop envy from arriving; a cousin's news, a friend's win, and there it is.

teach.h: NAME THE ENEMY BEFORE IT FINDS A HELPER.
teach.b: The Hindu move is to name the enemy when it shows up, before it finds its Shakuni.

how: In Hindu retellings of the Mahabharata, Shakuni is known as the master of the dice, and the conversation on the road is told as the moment Duryodhana's envy becomes a plan.

s: Duryodhana claimed the Pandavas had cheated him
he said their prosperity itself was what he couldn't bear.
Hindu teachers call envy one of six inner enemies
the shadripu: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy (matsarya).
Shakuni proposed attacking the Pandavas in battle
he said they were too strong to beat that way, and offered dice instead.

games.q: your friend is happy for you, mostly, but your good news clearly stings. in the language of the six inner enemies, what's she fighting?
games.why: matsarya is envy: someone else's good fortune felt as your own wound. it's the enemy that rode home with Duryodhana.

practice: Is there someone whose good fortune is hard to watch right now, a friend's news, a sibling's easy road?

Let the name come, and call the sting what Hindu teachers call it: matsarya, envy, an enemy inside, not the truth about them or you. Then say for them a prayer many Hindus know: sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all be happy.
Say it slowly, with their name in it. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, three times, and mean it a little more each time.

wordCard.voice: Envy, matsarya in Sanskrit, the last of the six inner enemies: taking someone else's good fortune as your own wound. Today Duryodhana speaks it aloud, and Shakuni answers with a plan.

orig.note: Sanskrit akṣa: a die, one of the dice used in the game.

carryVoice: Your line: envy is one of the six inner enemies. Name it when it comes. Day seven hundred sixty-five, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana confesses his grief to Shakuni; Shakuni proposes the dice game)
